claims.claim: Aeschylus quoted verbatim from E. D. A. Morshead, The House of Atreus (1881; Morshead d. 1912), Gutenberg #8604 (header checked: 'Translator: E. D. A. Morshead'). Spec's #8714 was wrong. Extracted by extract.py; Gutenberg italic underscores removed (formatting only). Greek line numbers assigned by matching content (Morshead has none): Ag. 1–39, 160–183, 184–257, 1560–1566; Eum. 582–613, 681–710, 734–753, 778–807, 881–902.

Sophocles quoted verbatim from F. Storr (Loeb, 1912; Storr d. 1919), Gutenberg #31 (header: 'Translator: Francis Storr'), because the Jebb Perseus files failed to fetch. Greek lines matched by content: OT 1–150, 1182–1222, 1329–1335, 1369–1385; OC 960–988; Ant. 162–210, 332–375, 441–525.

Euripides, Bacchae: T. A. Buckley's prose (Bohn, 1850; Buckley d. 1856) in the Perseus TEI file perseus-eng2, header 'Bacchae Modernized by Perseus ... T. A. Buckley ... London Henry G. Bohn 1850'; Perseus line numbers used. Lines 1–63, 1111–1124 (from the messenger's speech), 1259–1300, 1301–1328, 1330–1351.
Aristotle, Poetics IV, VI, XIII, XIV verbatim from S. H. Butcher (1895; d. 1910), Gutenberg #1974.
A. C. Bradley, Shakespearean Tragedy (1904; Bradley d. 1935), Lecture I, verbatim from Gutenberg #16966; original English, author died before 1955.

Scripture from the WEB via web.py: Hebrews 5:7–9; 12:7–11; Deuteronomy 19:1–13; Acts 5:27–32; Hosea 11:3–9; quoted verses Psalm 8:4–5, Jeremiah 17:9, Acts 17:23, Luke 23:34, John 1:11, 14, John 20:27, Matthew 27:46, 54, Romans 8:22, Amos 5:12, 24, Mark 7:21–23, 1 John 1:8.
City Dionysia: three tragedians, three tragedies and a satyr play each; choregia; judges chosen by lot; orphans' parade and allied tribute before the plays.
claims.source: Pickard-Cambridge, Dramatic Festivals of Athens (2nd ed. 1968); Goldhill, JHS 107 (1987)

claims.claim: Victories: Aeschylus 13, Sophocles 18 (some sources 20 or 24), Euripides 4 in his lifetime (a fifth posthumously).
Theatre capacity 6,000 to over 15,000 (estimates); Athenian adult male citizens perhaps 30,000–50,000 in the 5th century.
Thirty-two complete tragedies survive: 7 Aeschylus (Prometheus disputed), 7 Sophocles, 18 or 19 Euripides (Rhesus disputed).
Aeschylus fought at Marathon (490 BC), where his brother Cynegirus died; his epitaph mentions Marathon only; died in Sicily 456 BC.
claims.source: Herodotus 6.114; Life of Aeschylus; Pausanias 1.14.5; Athenaeus 14.627c

claims.claim: Athenaeus 8.347e: Aeschylus called his tragedies 'slices from the great banquets of Homer'.
Herodotus I.207: Croesus says his sufferings have been his lessons.
Robert F. Kennedy, Indianapolis, 4 April 1968, quoted Agamemnon in Edith Hamilton's translation ('the awful grace of God'); the city stayed largely calm.
claims.source: Text of the speech (JFK Library); Edith Hamilton, The Greek Way (1930)

claims.claim: Hebrews 5:8 'emathen aph' hōn epathen' echoes the pathein/mathein proverb.
claims.source: Hebrews 5:8 Greek text; standard commentaries (e.g. Attridge, Hermeneia 1989)

claims.claim: Ephialtes' reforms 462/461 BC; Ephialtes assassinated soon after.
Draco's homicide law c. 621 BC distinguished intentional and unintentional killing; republished 409/408 BC (IG I³ 104).
claims.source: R. S. Stroud, Drakon's Law on Homicide (1968)

claims.claim: A tie vote acquits ('the vote of Athena') became Athenian practice.
Froma Zeitlin, 'The Dynamics of Misogyny', Arethusa 11 (1978); E. R. Dodds, 'Morals and Politics in the Oresteia' (1960).
Sophocles born Colonus c. 496 BC; general 441/440 with Pericles; over 120 plays; OT probably 420s; OC staged posthumously 401 BC.
claims.source: Life of Sophocles; Plutarch, Pericles 8; Androtion fr.; standard

claims.claim: Plague at Athens 430–426 BC; Pericles died 429 BC.
Aristotle thought Oedipus the model tragedy (Poetics XIII, XIV and passim).
E. R. Dodds, 'On Misunderstanding the Oedipus Rex', Greece & Rome 13 (1966); Bernard Knox, Oedipus at Thebes (1957); Vernant, 'Ambiguity and Reversal' (1970).
Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams (1899, dated 1900), ch. V, on Oedipus.
Aristotle, Rhetoric I.13 (1373b) and I.15 (1375a–b) cite Antigone's unwritten laws.
Antigone 672: anarchy the worst of evils.
Aquinas, ST I–II q.95 a.2: a law contrary to natural law is 'a perversion of law'; quoted in substance by King, Letter from Birmingham Jail (16 April 1963).
Hegel on Antigone: Phenomenology (1807); Lectures on Aesthetics ('one of the most sublime ... works of art').
claims.source: Hegel, Aesthetics, tr. Knox (1975) II, p. 1218

claims.claim: Anouilh's Antigone premiered Paris, February 1944; Brecht's Antigone 1948 (Chur), prologue set in Berlin 1945; Heaney, The Burial at Thebes (2004); George Steiner, Antigones (1984).
Simone Weil, 'Antigone' (1936) for Entre nous, the factory bulletin at Rosières; in Intimations of Christianity among the Ancient Greeks (1957).
Ambrose barred Theodosius after the massacre of Thessalonica (390), Letter 51; Thomas More's last words 'the king's good servant, but God's first' (1535).
claims.source: Ambrose; the Paris News Letter report

claims.claim: Euripides: c. 480–406 BC; died in Macedonia; Bacchae staged posthumously, won first prize; Hippolytus 428; Trojan Women 415, after Melos (416/415).
claims.source: Life of Euripides; scholia to Frogs 67; Thucydides V.84–116

claims.claim: Euripides fr. 292 (Bellerophon): 'if gods do anything shameful, they are not gods'.
claims.source: Nauck fr. 292.7; Collard & Cropp, Loeb Euripides VII

claims.claim: Dodds, Euripides: Bacchae (1944; 2nd ed. 1960); Greeks and the Irrational (1951); Verrall, The Bacchants of Euripides (1910).
Nietzsche, Birth of Tragedy (1872): Apollonian/Dionysian; tragedy justifies existence 'only as an aesthetic phenomenon'; blames Euripides and Socrates.
Bernard Williams, Shame and Necessity (1993); Girard, Violence and the Sacred (1972) discusses the Bacchae.
A page is lost after Bacchae 1329; Christus Patiens preserves lines used to reconstruct Agave's lament; Christus Patiens attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus, date and author uncertain.
Luke 23:34 is absent from some early manuscripts (e.g. P75, B).
Catharsis: Bernays (1857) purgation; Golden, TAPA 93 (1962) clarification; Politics VIII.7 promises an account in the Poetics.
Plato, Republic X 595a–608b against the tragic poets; Tertullian, De spectaculis; Augustine, Confessions III.2.
Steiner, The Death of Tragedy (1961); Sayers, 'The Greatest Drama Ever Staged' (1938); MacKinnon; Rowan Williams, The Tragic Imagination (2016).

Paintings described only from NGA assistivetext: Sarazin de Belmont, The Roman Theater at Taormina (1828); Fuseli, Oedipus Cursing His Son Polynices (1786); Tiepolo, Bacchus and Ariadne (c. 1743/1745); Moretto da Brescia, Pietà (1520s). All four claimed for tragedy in claims.jsonl.
